item.text: {"text":"Recent research supports separating evidence of rejection from absent interaction. *Evidence Before Sampling* (2026 preprint) explicitly distinguishes the validity of negative labels from downstream recommendation performance; missing interactions alone cannot establish disinterest or its cause. Netflix’s *Lifecycle of LLM-as-a-Judge* (2026 preprint) describes criterion-specific rubrics, human labels with rationales, and ongoing human alignment for recommendation explanations—useful methodological precedent, though not validation of simulated purchase willingness. *AbstentionBench* (2025) finds that prompting improves abstention without reliably resolving uncertainty. Sources: [negative-label evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07708), [recommendation judging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.18300), [abstention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09038).\n\nPractical synthesis for the twenty training users: annotate each recommendation with explicit willingness to choose (yes/no/unknown), plus separate evidence-backed reasons for rejection: duplication, incompatibility, quantity mismatch, stated intent/relevance mismatch, and mood mismatch. Attach the supporting feedback quotation or history/title/description/timestamp reference; distinguish user statements from annotator interpretations. Histories establish prior interaction, not ownership, satisfaction, current need, or mood; unsupported judgments remain unknown. Independently double-annotate, report raw agreement and chance-corrected agreement per reason, and report coverage as supported judgments divided by all recommendations. Connect reasons to ranking through rejection counts at each rank and reason-specific rates among assessable top-k items, always displaying denominators and unknown rates. These are proposed diagnostic measures, not established findings or replacements for the fixed macro validation HR@10; twenty users support exploratory diagnosis, not population-level conclusions."}
